idiom_name: public final method delegating to protected primitives (Template Method shape)
implementation_notes: Java methods are virtual by default, so the non-virtual half must be written explicitly: declare the public operation `final` (the Java tutorial: a final method cannot be overridden by subclasses) and keep the variant step in a protected hook that is abstract or has a default body - the shape used throughout the JDK's collection framework (public operations built on abstract get(int)/size()). `final` supplies exactly the guarantee C++ gets from non-virtual-by-default; the hook stays protected because a subclass must be able to implement it.
pitfalls: Without `final` the wrapper is virtual again and any subclass - or a mocking framework - can replace it; the modifier is the guarantee, not a style choice.
Calling an overridable hook from a constructor runs before the subclass fields are initialised.
A subclass may widen a protected hook to public (visibility may be increased on override), which re-exposes the extension point to clients.

variants.name: Closed hierarchy: sealed base with final entry points (Java 17)
variants.idiom_name: sealed class/interface with permits + final wrapper
variants.implementation_notes: When the set of implementations is known, `sealed` (JEP 409, Java 17) states it in the type system: only the permitted subclasses may extend the base, every permitted subclass must be final, sealed or non-sealed, and the JVM rejects unauthorised subclasses when the class is loaded. Combined with a final public entry point this turns the non-virtual contract from a naming discipline into a checked closed world - and makes pattern-matching switches over the hierarchy exhaustive. Use it for library hierarchies that were never meant to be extended by clients.
pitfalls: Permitted subtypes must live in the same module (and package, in the unnamed module), so sealing constrains packaging, not only design.
Sealing freezes extension: adding an implementation later is a source change in the base class, not a client-side addition.
A permitted subtype declared `non-sealed` re-opens that branch of the hierarchy to arbitrary subclasses - almost always wrong for an invariant-bearing base.
